anathema

uh-NATH-uh-muh · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Anathema is a thing or person that is intensely disliked or detested.

Silence during a movie was anathema to her -- she couldn't sit through a single scene without whispering commentary.

Example

To the minimalist architect, ornate decoration of any kind was anathema; even a single decorative molding was enough to make him walk out of a project.

Anathema names a thing that is intensely disliked or detested -- the architect doesn't just dislike ornate decoration, he treats it as something to be avoided entirely.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bane: A bane is a thing that causes real trouble or misery -- weeds are the bane of a gardener, the thing that plagues them. Anathema is about detestation rather than damage: a thing someone finds so offensive they refuse to tolerate it, whether or not it ever harms them.

aversion: An aversion is the feeling of strong dislike inside you -- you have an aversion to crowds. Anathema names the thing itself, the object that feeling points at: crowds are anathema to you. The aversion is the reaction; the anathema is what provokes it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

delight: great pleasure

favorite: a person or thing especially liked

Where it sits · how strong the negative feeling is

dislike → anathema → abomination

dislike vs. anathema: Dislike is far milder than anathema -- dislike is an everyday negative preference, something you simply avoid when convenient. Anathema is detestation hardened into refusal: a thing someone will not tolerate at all.

abomination vs. anathema: An abomination is even stronger than anathema -- a thing that is anathema to you is one you personally detest and refuse to accept, while an abomination is so morally horrifying that nearly everyone recoils from it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ana-: up, back, again (Greek)

root — thema: something placed or set down; a thing set apart (Greek tithenai, 'to place')

Put it together: Anathema comes from Greek ana- ('back, apart') + tithenai ('to place') -- originally 'a thing set apart' (as a curse), which came to mean something intensely disliked.

Use the root in a new word: thesis: Her senior thesis argued that the two ancient trade routes had actually merged much earlier than historians believed.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Anathema names the object of intense dislike -- 'X is anathema to Y' -- which makes it grammatically different from abhorrent (an adjective describing a thing's own repulsive quality) and from misanthrope (a person who dislikes people in general, not one specific thing).
